danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: Da grevinden (grevindens Rostova) fik besked om Natasjas sygdom, rejste hun, skønt endnu ikke helt rask og stadig svag, til Moskva med Petja og resten af husholdningen, og hele familien flyttede fra Márja Dmítrievnas hus til deres eget og slog sig ned i byen.

Natasjas sygdom var så alvorlig, at betragtningen af alt det, der havde forårsaget den — hendes opførsel og den brudte forlovelse — heldigvis for hende og hendes forældre trådte i baggrunden. Hun var så syg, at det var umuligt for dem at overveje, i hvor høj grad hun selv bar skyld for det skete. Hun kunne ikke spise eller sove, tabte sig synligt, hostede, og lægerne lod dem som bekendt forstå, at hun var i fare. De kunne ikke tænke på andet end at hjælpe hende. Lægerne kom enkeltvis og i konsultation, talte meget på fransk, tysk og latin, bebrejdede hinanden og forskrev et stort udvalg af medicin for alle de sygdomme, de kendte til, men den enkle tanke faldt aldrig nogen af dem ind, at de ikke kunne kende den sygdom, Natasja led af, da ingen sygdom hos et levende menneske kan kendes, for ethvert levende væsen har sine egne særpræg og altid sin egen særlige, personlige, nye, komplicerede sygdom, ukendt for lægevidenskaben — ikke en sygdom i lunger, lever, hud, hjerte, nerver og så videre, som nævnes i lægernes bøger, men en sygdom, der består af en af de utallige kombinationer af disse organers lidelser. Denne enkle tanke kunne ikke falde lægerne ind (ligesom det ikke kan falde en troldmand ind, at han er ude af stand til at udføre sine kunster), fordi det var deres livsgerning at helbrede, de modtog penge for det og havde tilbragt deres bedste år med den opgave. Men frem for alt holdt denne tanke sig borte fra deres sind, fordi de indså, at de virkelig var nyttige, og det var de i sandhed for hele familien Rostov. Deres nytte beroede ikke på, at de fik patienten til at sluge stoffer, der for det meste var skadelige (skaden var knap mærkbar, da de blev givet i små doser), men de var nyttige, nødvendige og uundværlige, fordi de tilfredsstillede et sjæleligt behov hos den syge og hos dem, der elskede hende — og derfor findes og altid vil findes kvaksalvere, kloge koner, homøopater og allopater. De tilfredsstillede det evige menneskelige behov for håb om lindring, for medfølelse, og for at der gøres noget, et behov som føles af dem, der lider. De tilfredsstillede det behov, man ser i sin mest elementære form hos et barn, når det vil have et sted gnedet, der er gjort ondt. Et barn slår sig og løber straks hen i sin mors eller sin barnepiges arme for at få det ømme sted gnedet eller kysset, og det føler sig bedre tilpas, når det er gjort. Barnet kan ikke tro, at de stærkeste og viseste af dets nærmeste ikke har nogen kur mod dets smerte, og håbet om lindring og udtrykket af moderens medfølelse, mens hun gnubber bulen, trøster det. Lægerne var til nytte for Natasja, fordi de kyssede og gnubbede hendes bule og forsikrede hende om, at det snart ville gå over, bare kusken kørte hen til apotekeren på Arbát og hentede en pulver og nogle piller i en pæn æske til en rubel og halvfjerds kopek, og bare hun tog disse pulvere opløst i kogt vand med nøjagtigt to timers mellemrum, hverken mere eller mindre.

Hvad ville Sonja og greven og grevinden have gjort, hvordan ville de have set ud, hvis intet var blevet gjort, hvis der ikke havde været de piller at give efter uret, de varme drikke, kyllingkoteletterne og alle de andre detaljer i hverdagen, som lægerne ordinerede, og hvis overholdelse gav familien beskæftigelse og trøst? Hvordan ville greven have båret sin højtelskede datters sygdom, hvis han ikke havde vidst, at den kostede ham tusind rubler, og at han ikke ville spare yderligere tusinder for at gavne hende, eller hvis han ikke havde vidst, at hvis hendes sygdom fortsatte, ville han uden at tøve bruge endnu andre tusinder og tage hende til udlandet til konsultation, og hvis han ikke havde kunnet forklare i detaljer, hvordan Métivier og Feller ikke havde forstået symptomerne, men Frise havde, og Múdrov havde diagnosticeret dem endnu bedre? Hvad ville grevinden have gjort, hvis hun ikke af og til kunne skælde den syge ud for ikke nøje at følge lægens ordrer?

»Du bliver aldrig rask på den måde,« plejede hun at sige og glemte sin sorg i sin irritation, »hvis du ikke adlyder lægen og tager din medicin til rette tid! Man skal ikke spøge med det, ved du, for det kan udvikle sig til lungebetændelse,« fortsatte hun og fandt megen trøst i at udtale dette fremmede ord, der var ligeså uforståeligt for andre som for hende selv.

Hvad ville Sonja have gjort uden den glade bevidsthed om, at hun ikke havde klædt sig af de første tre nætter for at være klar til at udføre alle lægens forskrifter med præcision, og at hun stadig lå vågen om natten for ikke at forsømme det rette tidspunkt, da de let skadelige piller i den lille forgyldte æske skulle gives? Selv for Natasja var det behageligt at se, at der blev bragt så mange ofre for hendes skyld, og at vide, at hun skulle tage medicin til bestemte tider, selv om hun erklærede, at ingen medicin ville kurere hende, og at det hele var nonsens. Og det var endog behageligt at kunne vise, ved at se bort fra ordrerne, at hun ikke troede på medicinsk behandling og ikke satte pris på sit liv.

Lægen kom hver dag, følte hendes puls, så på hendes tunge og spøgte med hende, uden at lade sig anfægte af hendes sorgfulde ansigt. Men når han var gået ind i et andet værelse, hvortil grevinden hastigt fulgte ham, antog han en alvorlig mine og sagde, idet han tankefuldt rystede på hovedet, at selv om der var fare, havde han forventninger til virkningen af den seneste medicin, og man måtte se tiden an, at sygdommen hovedsageligt var sjælelig, men... Og grevinden, idet hun forsøgte at skjule handlingen for sig selv og for ham, stak en guldmønt i hans hånd og vendte altid tilbage til patienten med et mere beroliget sind.

Symptomerne på Natasjas sygdom var, at hun spiste lidt, sov lidt, hostede og altid var nedtrykt. Lægerne sagde, at hun ikke kunne klare sig uden behandling, og de holdt hende derfor i byens kvalme luft, og familien Rostov flyttede ikke på landet den sommer 1812.

Trods de mange piller hun slugte og de dråber og pulvere i de små flasker og æsker, som Madame Schoss, der var glad for den slags ting, samlede en stor samling af, og trods at hun var berøvet det landliv, hun var vant til, sejrede ungdommen. Natasjas sorg begyndte at blive overlejret af hverdagens indtryk, den ophørte med at trykke så smertefuldt på hendes hjerte, den svandt gradvist hen i fortiden, og hun begyndte at komme sig fysisk.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: When the countess heard that Natasha was ill, she went to Moscow with Petya and the rest of the household, though she wasn't fully recovered herself and was still weak. The whole family moved from Marya Dmitrievna's house to their own and settled in town.

Natasha's illness was so serious that, fortunately for her and for her parents, everything that had caused it — her conduct and the breaking of her engagement — receded into the background. She was so ill that they couldn't consider how far she was to blame for what had happened. She couldn't eat or sleep, she grew visibly thinner and she coughed, and the doctors made them feel she was in danger. They could think of nothing but how to help her. Doctors came to see her singly and in consultation, talked a great deal in French, German and Latin, blamed one another, and prescribed a great variety of medicines for every disease they knew. But it never occurred to any of them that they could not know the disease Natasha was suffering from, just as no disease of a living person can be known. Every living person has his own peculiarities and always has his own peculiar, personal, new, complicated disease, unknown to medicine — not a disease of the lungs, liver, skin, heart, nerves and so on, as listed in medical books, but a disease made up of one of the countless combinations of the ailments of those organs. This simple thought could not occur to the doctors (just as it cannot occur to a wizard that he is unable to work his spells) because the business of their lives was to cure, they were paid for it, and they had spent the best years of their lives on it. Above all, though, that thought was kept out of their minds by seeing that they were really useful, as they truly were to the whole Rostov family. Their usefulness did not depend on making the patient swallow substances that were mostly harmful (the harm was hardly noticeable, since the doses were small). They were useful, necessary and indispensable because they met a mental need of the invalid and of those who loved her — and that is why there are, and always will be, pseudo-healers, wise women, homeopaths and allopaths. They met the eternal human need of those who suffer for hope of relief, for sympathy, and for something to be done. They met the need seen in its most elementary form in a child, who wants a hurt place rubbed. A child bumps itself and runs at once into the arms of its mother or nurse to have the sore spot rubbed or kissed, and it feels better once that is done. The child cannot believe that the strongest and wisest of its people have no remedy for its pain, and the hope of relief, together with its mother's sympathy as she rubs the bump, comforts it. The doctors were useful to Natasha because they kissed and rubbed her bump. They assured her it would soon pass if only the coachman went to the chemist's on the Arbat and got a powder and some pills in a pretty box for a ruble and seventy kopeks, and if she took those powders in boiled water at intervals of exactly two hours, neither more nor less.

What would Sonya, the count and the countess have done, how would they have looked, if nothing had been done? If there hadn't been those pills to give by the clock, the warm drinks, the chicken cutlets and all the other details of life prescribed by the doctors, whose carrying out gave the family circle something to do and some consolation? How would the count have borne his dearly loved daughter's illness if he hadn't known that it was costing him a thousand rubles, and that he wouldn't grudge thousands more to benefit her? If he hadn't known that, should her illness go on, he wouldn't grudge yet other thousands and would take her abroad for consultations there? If he hadn't been able to explain in detail how Metivier and Feller had failed to understand the symptoms, but Frise had understood them, and Mudrov had diagnosed them even better? What would the countess have done if she hadn't been able, now and then, to scold the invalid for not strictly obeying the doctor's orders?

"You'll never get well like this," she would say, forgetting her grief in her annoyance, "if you won't obey the doctor and take your medicine at the right time! You mustn't trifle with it, you know, or it may turn into pneumonia," she would go on, taking great comfort in saying that foreign word, which was incomprehensible to others and to herself too.

What would Sonya have done without the glad awareness that she hadn't undressed for the first three nights, so as to be ready to carry out all the doctor's instructions exactly, and that she still stayed awake at night so as not to miss the right time for giving the slightly harmful pills in the little gilt box? Even to Natasha herself it was pleasant to see that so many sacrifices were being made for her, and to know that she had to take medicine at fixed hours, though she declared that no medicine would cure her and that it was all nonsense. And it was even pleasant to be able to show, by disregarding the orders, that she didn't believe in medical treatment and didn't value her life.

The doctor came every day, felt her pulse, looked at her tongue and joked with her, paying no attention to her grief-stricken face. But when he had gone into another room, where the countess hurried after him, he put on a grave air. Shaking his head thoughtfully, he said that although there was danger, he had hopes of this latest medicine and they must wait and see; that the illness was mainly mental, but... And the countess, trying to hide what she was doing from herself and from him, slipped a gold coin into his hand and always went back to the patient with a calmer mind.

The symptoms of Natasha's illness were that she ate little, slept little, coughed, and was always low-spirited. The doctors said she couldn't manage without medical treatment, so they kept her in the stifling air of the town, and the Rostovs did not go to the country that summer of 1812.

She swallowed many pills and took drops and powders from the little bottles and boxes, of which Madame Schoss, who was fond of such things, had made a large collection. She was also deprived of the country life she was used to. In spite of all that, youth prevailed. Natasha's grief began to be covered over by the impressions of daily life, it stopped pressing so painfully on her heart, it gradually faded into the past, and she began to recover physically.
